posts.hook: Nobody told you it was a different job. That's not a metaphor — it's the actual problem.
posts.body:
You were the best engineer on the team. That's why they promoted you.

And now you're six weeks in, rehearsing what to say before your own standups, and the 1:1s feel like minefields.

Here's what I've watched happen to almost every engineer who makes this move:

They assume the skills that got them promoted are the skills the new job needs. They're not. Writing code is a solo act. Managing people is not.

The job you were actually promoted into has different problems. Different measures of success. A completely different relationship with being wrong.

The panic you feel at 2am — the certainty you've been found out — that's not evidence you were the wrong choice. It's a known feature of this transition. Every engineer who has moved through it started from exactly where you are.

The ones who come out the other side aren't the ones who waited for it to click. They're the ones who got permission to learn the new job out loud instead of pretending they already knew it.

posts.hook: If you're rehearsing what to say before your own standups, this is for you.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, plain background, no graphics]

If you're rehearsing what to say before your own standups — I want you to know that's not a you problem. That's what the engineer-to-manager transition actually feels like for most people.

You spent years getting good at a job where the feedback loop was fast. You wrote the code. It worked or it didn't. You fixed it.

Management doesn't work like that. The feedback is slow, ambiguous, and sometimes it comes in the form of your strongest engineer going quiet in meetings.

And nobody told you it was going to feel like this. Because nobody told you it was a different job.

I spent nine years as an engineering manager. I've had the redundancy conversations. I've shipped late. I've been the one in the stairwell.

The panic is normal. The good news is it has a known trajectory.

If you want to know what that looks like — more on that in the next video.

posts.hook: The 1:1 that went badly quiet. You've been replaying it ever since.
posts.body:
You know the one.

You asked how things were going. They said 'fine.' The silence that followed was a different kind of silence than you expected. And you did not know how to fill it without making it worse.

So you talked about sprint velocity.

Afterwards you sat with the feeling that something had gone wrong in that room and you didn't have the language for what it was or how to fix it.

Here's what I'd say to you:

That conversation didn't fail because you're a bad manager. It failed because nobody taught you what a 1:1 is actually for.

It isn't a status update. It isn't a performance check. It's the one place your direct report should be able to say the thing they're not saying in standup.

Your job in the room is to make it easier for them to speak than to stay quiet. That's a learnable skill. It has nothing to do with being the best engineer in the room.

I've watched engineers run that exact conversation badly in week two of our work together and run it well in week six. The gap isn't talent. It's knowing what you're actually trying to do.

posts.hook: How to give feedback to an engineer when you don't want to make it weird.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, conversational, no slides]

Giving feedback as a new engineering manager is uncomfortable. Here's why, and what to do about it.

Step one: name the behaviour, not the person. 'The PR had no tests and it blocked the release' lands differently than 'you're not being careful enough.' One is a fact. One is a verdict.

Step two: say it close to when it happened. Feedback stored up for a quarter review has lost most of its usefulness.

Step three: ask before you advise. 'What happened from your side?' before 'here's what you should do next time.' You will learn something almost every time you do this, and the conversation changes.

Step four: make it normal. If feedback only arrives when something went wrong, your team will dread it. If it's a regular part of how the team works — brief, specific, both directions — it stops being a big deal.

None of this requires a framework. It requires practice and someone to tell you when it landed and when it didn't.

That's most of what I do with engineers in the first four weeks.

posts.hook: How to handle a skip-level meeting when you haven't had one before.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, slightly leaning forward — this matters to them]

A skip-level is when your manager's manager meets with your team directly, without you in the room. Or sometimes with you in the room and the pressure is on to say something useful.

Either way — if you haven't been through one as a manager, here's what to know.

First: your team will be asked how you're doing. This is normal. It's not a trap. Stop treating it like one.

Second: if you're in the room, don't perform. The impulse is to prove you have it under control. That impulse is visible and it works against you. Say what you actually know. Say clearly what you're still figuring out.

Third: brief your team beforehand — not to coach their answers, but so they're not blindsided. One sentence. 'Sarah from the leadership team is meeting with you on Thursday to hear how things are going on the team.' That's it.

Fourth: after the skip-level, ask your manager what came out of it. Don't wait to be told. Asking is what managers who are on top of things do.

The engineers I coach who freeze in skip-levels aren't freezing because they're bad at their job. They're freezing because they've never been told what the room is actually for.

posts.hook: What to do in the first 30 days as an engineering manager — practically.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, brisk and grounded]

Thirty days in as an engineering manager. Here's what I'd actually focus on.

Week one: don't change anything. Seriously. Observe. Ask more questions than you answer. Your strongest instinct will be to fix things. Resist it.

Week two: do a proper 1:1 with everyone on the team. Not a status update — a listening session. What's working for them, what's frustrating them, what they need from you that they're not getting. Write down what they say.

Week three: pick one thing from those conversations that you can actually change. Not a big thing. A small, visible one. Do it. Tell them you did it because they said it.

Week four: have the conversation you've been putting off. You know the one. The direct report who's going quiet, the tension you've been talking around. Bring it up. You don't need a script. You need to name it.

None of this will feel comfortable. Comfortable is not the standard. Moving in the right direction is the standard.

posts.hook: How to handle a direct report who's going quiet in meetings.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, direct and practical]

Your strongest engineer has stopped contributing in standups. They answer questions with one word. In 1:1s they say everything's fine.

Here's what not to do: don't wait. Don't tell yourself it's a phase. Don't give them more technical challenges hoping it fixes it.

Here's what I'd actually do.

Step one: name it in the 1:1 — directly and without cushioning it. 'I've noticed you've been quieter in the last couple of weeks. What's going on?' Not 'are you okay?' — too easy to deflect. Name the specific thing you observed.

Step two: stop talking. This is harder than it sounds. After you ask, wait. The silence is uncomfortable. Sit in it.

Step three: listen to what they say without immediately problem-solving it. Whatever comes up — a frustration, a concern about the team, something about the work — hear it before you fix it.

Step four: follow up. Not in three weeks. In three days. 'I've been thinking about what you said. Here's what I want to do about it.'

The engineers who go quiet are almost always telling you something before they decide to tell someone else. Your job is to be easier to tell than the alternative.

posts.hook: The skip-level meeting where I said nothing useful for four minutes. Here's what I learned.
posts.body:
I've been in the stairwell.

I mean that literally. Early in my time as an engineering manager, there was a skip-level where the VP asked me a question about my team's velocity and why it had dropped. I knew the answer. I knew what had gone wrong and what we were doing about it.

And I froze. I talked around it for four minutes without saying anything useful. Then I went and stood in the stairwell afterwards and felt like the worst manager in the building.

Here's what I know now that I didn't know then:

I wasn't prepared because I didn't know what prepared looked like in that room. I thought the job was to perform certainty — to project control. It isn't. The job is to know what's true, say it clearly, and be honest about what you're still working on.

Managers who are honest about what they're working on build more trust than ones who perform omniscience. Even when 'what they're working on' is a team that's struggling.

The skip-level freeze is almost universal in the first year. The engineers I coach aren't freezing because they're bad managers. They're freezing because nobody showed them what that room was actually for.

posts.hook: Why engineers make the transition harder than it needs to be.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, slightly wry but direct]

Engineers are, professionally, very good at not admitting they don't know something.

It's a reasonable survival strategy when you're an individual contributor. Uncertainty in a code review costs you credibility. Being wrong in a production incident costs you trust.

But in management, that same instinct — project certainty, don't show the gap, wait until you know before you speak — makes everything slower and harder.

The engineers I work with who move through this transition fastest are not the most technically capable ones. They're the ones who, at some point, decide that learning the job out loud is better than waiting to already know it.

Admitting to a direct report that you don't have the answer and you're going to find out is not weakness. It's what managing people actually looks like.

Your team already knows you're figuring it out. They knew before you did. What they're waiting to see is whether you'll admit it.

When you do — something shifts. One client put it plainly: the weird thing was his team seemed to like him more once he stopped pretending to have all the answers.

That's the move. And it's available to you right now.

posts.hook: How to run a 1:1 that's actually useful — for both of you.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, practical and grounded]

Most new engineering managers run 1:1s like status updates. Here's how to make them useful instead.

First: the agenda is theirs, not yours. Before the meeting, send them a prompt — 'What do you want to cover this week?' — and build the conversation around what comes back. If nothing comes back, that's information.

Second: start with what's going well. Not as a warm-up, but genuinely. What has actually worked this week? Spend two minutes there. It calibrates the conversation.

Third: ask the question behind the question. 'How's the sprint going?' usually means 'how are you going?' Ask both. They're different.

Fourth: have one thing you're going to follow up on by the next 1:1. Not a list. One thing. Do it. Tell them you did it.

Fifth: end with a direct question — 'Is there anything I could be doing differently for you?' You will get non-answers at first. Keep asking. The answers come.

None of this is complicated. What makes it hard is doing it consistently, through the weeks when it feels pointless or awkward, until it becomes the thing your team counts on.

That's the job.

posts.hook: Engineers promoted into management after this year's performance reviews: this is for you.
posts.body:
Somewhere this month, someone heard on a Friday that they were now a manager. They face their team on Monday with no model for what the job actually requires.

If that's you — or if it's someone in your network — here's what I'd want you to know.

The panic is normal. Not 'it will pass' normal. Known, documented, experienced by nearly every engineer who has made this move. The 2am certainty that you've been found out is not evidence you were the wrong choice.

The job you've just been given is different from the job you were doing. The skills that got you promoted — being the best engineer in the room — are not the skills the new job runs on. That's not a criticism. It's just a thing nobody tells you.

You don't have to figure this out by finishing the management book or waiting for the e-learning to land. You can learn the job you were actually promoted into, out loud, with someone who has been in that role and remembers what the deep end feels like.

The September 1:1 waitlist has a few spots remaining. I close it when it reaches ten names.

If your company has an L&D budget and you haven't claimed it — this is what it's for.

posts.hook: If you've been watching these videos and thinking 'this is exactly where I am' — here's what to do next.
posts.body:
[Scene: direct to camera, unhurried]

If you've been watching these videos and recognising yourself — the rehearsed standups, the 1:1s that feel like minefields, the 2am certainty that you've been found out — then you already know the problem.

The question is what you do with it.

Most engineers do one of two things. They wait, hoping it clicks on its own. Or they buy another book and get 40% through it.

Neither works quickly. Waiting is slow. Reading about difficult conversations is not the same as having one with someone in the room who can tell you what landed and what didn't.

I coach engineers through the job they were actually promoted into. Not with a framework. With the specific 1:1 that went wrong, the direct report who's gone quiet, the skip-level that's coming.

Nine years as an engineering manager. Engineers can tell within ten minutes.

One client wrote to me after six weeks: "I cried a bit after session two. In a good way. Nobody had ever told me the panic was normal."

The September 1:1 waitlist is in the description. It has a few spots left.

If the panic is already real — that's the right time to start.
